The five grids analyzed were all 177 x 53 in size, chosen based on requirements for 3D Navier-Stokes analyses.
Grid A was generated using the GRAPE code, while grids B-E used a two-step process with an embedded viscous grid.
Grids C-E differed in their treatment of the matching condition along the cut line between the trailing edge and downstream boundary.

The heat transfer predictions were in good agreement with experimental data for the low turbulence intensity case (1%), but showed more sensitivity to transition modeling assumptions for the high turbulence intensity case (6%).
Reducing the near-wall grid spacing by a factor of 4 did not significantly improve the heat transfer predictions.

The pitchwise variation in total pressure was predicted less accurately than the heat transfer, with the grids enforcing matching along the cut line (A-D) showing a narrower wake and lower minimum total pressure compared to the experimental data.
Grid E, with a bent downstream boundary, showed better agreement with the experimental wake profile, but this may have been due to numerical diffusion from the coarser grid on the suction side.
Using a two-equation turbulence model (Chien's model) resulted in a wider wake prediction compared to the Baldwin-Lomax model, but did not significantly change the depth of the wake.
The overall loss coefficients calculated using the two flow solvers were reasonably close to the experimental value of 0.029, with the best agreement using grid D.
Over 50 spanwise grid planes are needed to achieve grid-independent heat transfer results for a typical turbine blade, limiting the maximum size of blade-to-blade grids to around 10,000 points.
